A Los Angeles neighbor could soon be punished for repeatedly feeding a coyote that mauled a toddler in a terrifying attack earlier this month.

The California Department of Fish and Wildlife said it launched an investigation into reports of someone illegally feeding the wild animal after a 16-month old was attacked on Oct. 16 in Atwater Village.

“CDFW wildlife officers investigated reports of Atwater Village residents feeding coyotes,” spokesperson Cort Klopping told The Post.

“Wildlife officers made contact with an individual that lives in the area and will be filing a case with the city’s attorney’s office for the illegal feeding of wildlife,” he added.

The agency said there was no further information they could share as the investigation is still ongoing. The illegal feeding of wildlife in Los Angeles carries a misdemeanor charge, if pursued by the city.

Last Friday, CDFW officials responded to the 3300 block of Glenhurst Avenue following the attack on the toddler.

The child was then rushed to a local hospital for treatment and then released.

Officials did not disclose exactly what happened, describing the incident only as one in which a child was injured “after an incident involving a coyote.” That same evening, wildlife officers located a coyote in the vicinity and euthanized the animal, according to the department.

Investigators collected DNA samples from both the child and the coyote to determine whether the animal was responsible for the attack.

“DNA samples that were collected from the victim and the coyote that was taken have been analyzed and have confirmed the coyote that was taken is the offending animal,” according to a CDFW statement, NBC4 News reported.

The incident reignited concerns about coyotes roaming the neighborhood, where residents previously reported troubling encounters with an animal known as “Wiley.” In August, the coyote was spotted wandering through Atwater Village and was reportedly seen chasing children, raising fears among locals about the animal’s behavior, CBS Los Angeles reported.

Some residents suspected someone in the neighborhood had been feeding the wild animal.

“We’ve run into the coyote maybe a few times a week. Every time we go walking,” Libby Stankaitis, a local resident, told CBS Los Angeles.

The California Department of Fish and Wildlife warned residents that feeding wildlife is illegal and urged them to secure their properties and remove anything that could attract coyotes.

It remains unclear whether the coyote euthanized was Wiley, the animal that had prompted earlier concerns.

Wildlife officials recommend that residents maintain a safe distance from coyotes and slowly back away if they encounter one. Adults should keep young children and pets close, make loud noises and wave their arms to appear larger if a coyote approaches.

If a coyote makes physical contact, officials advise fighting back and contacting animal control or calling 911.

The California Department of Fish and Wildlife said it launched an investigation into reports of someone illegally feeding the wild animal after a 16-month old was attacked on Oct. 16 in Atwater Village.

“CDFW wildlife officers investigated reports of Atwater Village residents feeding coyotes,” spokesperson Cort Klopping told The Post.

“Wildlife officers made contact with an individual that lives in the area and will be filing a case with the city’s attorney’s office for the illegal feeding of wildlife,” he added.

news.originalContent:

WASHINGTON — Karoline Leavitt weighed in on her first successor to the White House press secretary job, saying the position “was not for” Katie Zacharia.

Leavitt told Fox News that being President Trump’s spokesperson “takes a lot of preparation and sometimes you don’t know how someone will perform until they go out there.”

“We wish Katie the best. The job obviously was not for her, but we wish her and her family well,” she added.

Zacharia lasted five days as Trump’s press secretary, giving a short briefing where she was visibly nervous. Since her departure, she returned to her California home and has stayed quiet, being captured in public working out and again sporting a MAGA hat.

But Zacharia’s supporters are crying foul about Leavitt’s not-so-subtle assessment.

“It’s unfair for the former press secretary to continue brutalizing President Trump’s hand-picked successor,” a source familiar with Zacharia’s thinking told The Post.

“Katie has been adamant about not taking any interviews with friendly or hostile press, has declined profile pieces and would like for the coverage to focus on President Trump’s hard work,” the source continued. “She will not go on a self-promotion tour because it does not benefit the president. And she remains ruthlessly loyal while facing unprecedented attacks against her.”

Behind the scenes, some of the administration concedes that Zacharia was given a tough start.

She flew in from California to interview with President Trump on the Friday before she started the job, then flew back to California to pack up her belongings and returned to Washington DC that weekend. Monday was spent onboarding — filling out the paperwork and background information necessary to work for the government.

Her first briefing was Tuesday morning, which was essentially her first full day on the job and she was sent into the press room to take on the media.

“I have always been deeply thankful for the opportunity to support President Trump and his agenda in the media in the years before he asked me to serve as Press Secretary,” Zacharia told The Post.

“There is no other president in history like him. He has single-handedly saved America with his effective policies, and no one has been more relentlessly attacked by the media than President Trump.”

She continued: “He deserves fair coverage of the real wins he is delivering for Americans — historic border security, massive new investments in manufacturing and energy, and the women’s health initiative he and the First Lady just launched. I continue to fully support the incredible work he is doing for the American people and for America’s interests around the world.”

The administration is not expected to hire a new press secretary before November’s midterm election.

“I wouldn’t expect anything new pre-midterms,” a source familiar told The Post.

Leavitt said she’s helping the president find a new person to fulfill one of the most public-facing roles in the administration, which she called “one of the hardest jobs in politics.”

“I’ve offered my help to the president to help him select someone who can serve him and the country well,” she told Fox.

But she declined to offer a list of names being considered for the role.

“I’ll keep my private counsel to the president private, but I do obviously talk to him about what the job entails, and he knows it very well. Nobody understands the press better than Donald Trump. He knows he needs someone who is tough, who is smart, who understands his policies, who is loyal, and who can go out there and put up a fight,” Leavitt said.

“There’s plenty of people who want the job… It’s just up to the president to make that decision.”

Leavitt received rave reviews for her work as press secretary. She stepped down in August to spend more time with her family, which includes two young children.

But she’s sticking with Team Trump, working for the president’s political arm as a spokesperson.

She was in Manchester, N.H., on Wednesday to speak to the Make the Heaven Crowded Tour, where she discussed how she prepared for her press briefings.

“I prepared like heck for that first briefing especially,” Leavitt said. “I poured myself into my preparation. I read. I studied. I talked to every cabinet member. I talked to the president.”

Leavitt also spoke to Pod Force One’s Miranda Devine late last year about standing at the podium in the briefing room.

“The press briefing room can be combative, and sometimes it is behind the scenes as well, but I tell our team that we need to be professional and get them facts, and nobody does that better than President Trump,” she said.

Zacharia, meanwhile, told The California Post she had no regrets.

“I’m proud I said yes, stood firm in what I believe, and kept supporting the president even when the circumstances weren’t ideal for me — showing my children what courage looks like in the face of criticism,” she said.

news.originalContent:
See more of our coverage in your search results.

The world’s richest man is launching his support behind Republican New York Rep. Mike Lawler.

Elon Musk’s self-financed America Super PAC dumped $600,000 to back Lawler in recent days as the two-term Hudson Valley congressman faces a tough challenge from Democrat Cait Conley in next month’s midterms, Federal Elections Commission filings show.

It’s a strong indication that Musk, the owner of SpaceX, Tesla and X Corp., will spend more than a million dollars in the campaign’s final days to bolster Lawler and slam Conley.

The Musk spending so far covers contracts to StoryTellers LLC for printing, postage and other messaging supporting Lawler and opposing Conley, the FEC filings, first reported by Gothamist, said.

Musk is the biggest single donor of the 2026 midterm elections, spending nearly $400 million this cycle, including more than $276 million since July, to help Republicans.

“It’s no surprise that Elon Musk has spent millions to keep his puppet Mike Lawler in office,” said Conley campaign spokesperson Maddy Rosen.

“Musk is the operator of the largest data center in the world, and Lawler cast the deciding vote to give data center operators $80 billion in tax breaks, while voting to ban states from regulating data centers and AI operations. As always, when it comes to Mike Lawler’s disastrous record, just follow the money.”

Lawler campaign spokesperson Ciro Riccardi responded, “By law, Lawler for Congress can’t coordinate with super PACs, and we have no say over what America PAC or any other outside group spends in this race.”

“Meanwhile, Cait Conley calls super PAC money ‘dark money,’ yet 27 outside groups, including a teachers’ union super PAC, VoteVets, and the League of Conservation Voters, have spent nearly $6.5 million to elect her. She even formed her own joint committee with House Majority PAC, a Washington super PAC, which has put millions into TV ads for her,” Riccardi said. “That’s hypocrisy.”

Another billionaire mogul, former three-term New York City Mayor Mike Bloomberg, is opening his wallet and spending $80 million to help Democrats re-take the House and Senate and win other races in the Nov. 3 elections.

Super PACs affiliated with President Trump, including MAGA Inc., could end up spending upwards of $400 million to help Republicans.

One Trump-aligned group, No Going Back PAC, has spent millions of dollars to help GOP challenger Mike LiPetri defeat Democratic Rep. Tom Suozzi in Long Island’s 3rd House District, as well as defend Lawler’s seat in the 17th House District.

Lawler, a former state assemblyman, is seeking a third-term to rep the district, which covers Westchester County from the White Plains border as far north as Hopewell Junction as well as Rockland, Putnam and Dutchess Counties.

Conley, an Army veteran and former Biden administration national security adviser, is making her first run for office.

The district was tightly contested in the 2024 election, too, with Lawler winning by a close 52% to 45% — and a razor-thin 50.3% to 49.7% against then-Democratic National Congressional Committee Chairman Sean Patrick Maloney in 2022.

Independent and internal party polls show the Lawler-Conley race is close and could be a nail-biter. Most political watchdogs have rated the race a toss-up.

Super PACS are independent expenditure groups that can raise and spend unlimited amounts of money to influence campaigns, unlike candidates’ campaign committees that face limits on how much can be raised from individual donors under federal law.

Christy Turlington’s first photo shoot was in 1983 at the age of 14 — yet she’s as booked and busy as ever today, 43 years later. While the OG supermodel has maintained a yoga habit for over 30 years, one thing she’s passing on is cosmetic surgery.

“I will never alter or augment my face. Never,” she told Vogue a few years back. However, she does lean into additional self-care, and for her, that includes a daily skin care regimen.

“I feel like I’ve earned and deserve better care when it comes to my skin, so everything is about bringing back moisture and treating myself well,” she shared.

Turlington found her go-to skin care line — Noble Panacea — long before partnering with the brand, and as such, it felt like a perfect match.

Founded by a Nobel Prize-winning chemist, Noble Panacea takes a science-forward approach to skin care, promising unparalleled results. The brand recently debuted its latest skin-perfecting innovation: The Exceptional RetiNAD+ Renewal Booster.

Made with a powerful retinoid complex that targets fine lines and wrinkles — plus loss of firmness and elasticity — the brand promises visible results in 10 days, with some seriously impressive before-and-after photos to back it up.

news.originalContent:
A new poll finds white evangelicals still outpace other demographic groups in supporting Trump, as he rallies the Republican base.

United States President Donald Trump’s support among white evangelical Protestant voters remains strong but has slipped since he retook office in January 2025, according to a new poll.

A survey released this month by the news agency Reuters and research firm Ipsos found that Trump’s support among the group had tumbled to 63 percent, down from 77 percent at the time of his second inauguration.

The shift comes as Trump’s approval rating drops to an all-time low of 31 percent.

White evangelicals are considered a key Republican demographic, and the decline could prove significant during the midterm elections on November 3, when the right-wing party will seek to defend its majorities in Congress.

Democrats remain widely favoured to take control of the US House of Representatives in the election. Their chances of flipping the Senate too are increasing amid widespread discontent over affordability and the US-Israeli war on Iran.

But experts say Republicans are counting on their base to counter signs of a Democratic surge at the polls.

On Wednesday, Trump campaigned in South Carolina, located in the southern “Bible Belt”, where exit polls found six in 10 Republican voters were white evangelicals in the 2024 presidential primary.

Trump carried the state by nearly 18 percentage points in the 2024 presidential election, but polls have shown Republican Senate candidate Darline Graham holding only a narrow lead over Democratic challenger Annie Andrews just two weeks ahead of the midterm vote.

As with many of his campaign appearances, Trump focused his South Carolina speech on several social issues that resonate with conservative Christians, including policies related to transgender people. During the rally, he referred to Andrews with an anti-transgender slur.

“She’s a fanatical transgender activist,” Trump said at a different point in his speech, despite Andrews skewing moderate on the issue within the Democratic Party. “How the hell do you run in South Carolina? Am I in a different state?”

Long a key demographic in Trump’s coalition, white evangelicals accounted for nearly a third of Trump’s winning coalition in 2024, according ⁠to a Public Religion Research Institute (PRRI) survey and a validated-voter analysis by the nonpartisan Pew Research Center.

The US president has been able to maintain support from key evangelical leaders despite a series of scandals at odds with the conservative values they espouse. Trump has faced allegations of sexual misconduct and extramarital affairs, which he denies.

All told, about 80 percent of white evangelical voters cast their ballots for Trump in the 2024 general election. The demographic makes up about 13 percent of the overall US population.

Beyond states like South Carolina, evangelicals in the Midwestern states of Iowa and Kansas, as well as the Southern state of Texas, could be key to the Republican Party maintaining its hold on the US Senate.

Christian faith leaders are challenging Republicans in several top races, including Adam Hamilton, a United Methodist Church pastor, in Kansas, and James Talarico, a Presbyterian seminarian, in Texas.

Both Hamilton and Talarico represent mainline Protestant denominations, not evangelical ones.

White evangelicals’ voter trends are distinct from other evangelical groups. For example, Black Protestant evangelicals, a vanguard of the US civil rights movement, have remained a key Democratic voting bloc.

Still, support for Trump among evangelicals remains strong compared with other demographic groups.

It remains unclear if shifting attitudes towards Trump would affect conservative turnout during the midterm elections, in which the US president is not on the ballot.

The Reuters news agency noted that white evangelicals were the only demographic it tracks that surpassed 60 percent support for Trump in the final stretch of the midterms.

The drop in support among the group was less pronounced than for Trump’s overall approval rating, tumbling 14 percentage points compared with a 16-point decline among Americans overall.

news.originalContent:
Health officials are investigating where Nigeria’s first patient, confirmed this week, was infected.

The World Health Organization (WHO) says the Ebola outbreak that emerged in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is growing more “complex”, with cases now present in countries in East and West Africa.

This comes as health authorities investigate where Nigeria’s first case, which was confirmed this week, originated, raising questions about whether the patient crossed paths with Kenya’s first patient at a Ugandan airport.

“We are facing a more complex outbreak landscape,” Mohamed Janabi, regional director for WHO in Africa, told an online media briefing on Thursday.

Nigeria reported its first case of the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola on Tuesday, becoming the fourth ⁠African country and the most populous yet to be affected by an outbreak that was announced in DRC in mid-May and has since killed more than 4,000 people there.

Kenya, DRC and Nigeria all have active or recent cases of the Bundibugyo strain, while Uganda had cases earlier in the year but has since been declared Ebola-free.

The Nigeria patient is the Ugandan-born wife of a Swiss diplomat based in Abuja. Authorities in Uganda said she had travelled to eastern DRC before transiting through Uganda. But the WHO and Africa’s top health agency said on ⁠Thursday they had not received confirmed information that the woman travelled to the DRC.

A Swiss government statement to the Reuters news agency also said the patient is believed to have contracted the disease while travelling in Uganda.

Wessam Mankoula, the head of Emergency Preparedness and Response at the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC), said on Thursday that both the first Nigerian case and the first Kenyan case had left Entebbe on October 3, and that a possible encounter between them was under investigation.

Ugandan authorities rejected the suggestion that she was infected in the country. Government spokesman Alan Kasujja told the AFP news agency that it was “preposterous” to link Uganda to the case simply because she had holidayed there.

However, Mankoula said there was no validated information that she had been to DRC, and Jean Kaseya, the Africa CDC director general, said the same. Pavel Ursu, the WHO representative in Nigeria, said the information given to the organisation included no travel outside Uganda.

Patrick Otim, a WHO emergency response manager, said on Thursday the source of her infection was still unknown as health authorities were working to piece together her travel history.

Investigators were looking at which Abuja health facilities she visited between the onset of symptoms and her hospitalisation 48 hours later, he added.

Kenya’s Ministry of Health confirmed its first case earlier this month and had reported eight more since. Patrick Amoth, the Health Ministry’s director-general, said officials had traced all 135 contacts of the first case.

Nigeria is now tracing 44 contacts, and Mankoula said more had since been identified but did not give a new number.

The current outbreak is the deadliest in DRC’s history, according to the country’s health authorities. It has killed more than 4,000 people out of more than 9,000 confirmed cases since May.

Neighbouring Uganda recorded 20 confirmed cases, including 15 imported from the DRC, and two deaths, before it was declared Ebola-free in August.

The Africa CDC has warned of an “extremely serious threat”, with the fatality rate in DRC approaching 50 percent.

news.originalContent:
Israeli court releases nine settler suspects over West Bank attacks as investigations into recent assaults continue.

Israel has released nine of the 10 Israeli settler suspects arrested over attacks on a US journalist and European diplomats in the occupied West Bank, placing them under house arrest.

An Israeli court in Jerusalem ordered the release late on Wednesday, according to Honenu, a law firm that represents Israeli settlers.

Israeli police said one suspect remained in custody and that the investigation into the violent incidents was continuing.

Masked settlers were filmed last week assaulting Heidi Levine, a Washington Post photojournalist covering a Palestinian olive harvest who was taken to hospital and underwent surgery on a finger.

In a separate attack earlier this week, masked settlers assaulted French, Belgian and Polish diplomats and a French mayor in another part of the West Bank.

The suspects had been detained after the United States called for a crackdown on settler violence. France, Belgium and Poland also urged Israel to act.

“In the vast majority of attacks against Palestinians, no arrests are made at all,” said Yonatan Kanonich, head of research at the Israeli rights group Yesh Din. “In cases that receive media coverage … the police arrest several settlers and release most of them shortly afterward.”

United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said in a post on X Thursday that the situation in the occupied Palestinian territory was “out of control”, with Palestinians continuing “to suffer daily attacks by Israeli settlers” and journalists and diplomats also being attacked.

Guterres called for “a credible political path towards lasting peace”.

Separately, the Palestinian Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission on Thursday said it documented 17 West Bank pogroms by Israeli forces and settlers against Palestinian farmers and their land during the olive harvest.

The commission recorded 409 attacks in October, 317 of which were by settlers and 92 by Israeli forces.

Nablus recorded the most attacks, 166, followed by Salfit with 91.

The commission said the attacks included assaults on farmers, preventing them from reaching their land, theft of crops and agricultural equipment, damage and burning of olive trees, as well as arrests, threats at gunpoint and live fire.

Ali Hassan Bazzari from Burqa died of wounds from settler gunfire while picking olives on October 7, the commission reported.

On Thursday, settlers set fire to olive trees near Imatin, east of Qalqilya, while Israeli forces forced farmers to leave and detained a farmer and several of his workers, the Palestinian news agency Wafa reported.

Near Yabad, west of Jenin, settlers stole 17 bags of harvested olives and equipment, local sources said.

Citing a local Palestinian official, Wafa reported that around Jenin, Israeli forces closed transport roads and most village gates, preventing farmers from reaching land in Barta’a.

news.originalContent:
NBA superstar LeBron James criticised by US President ⁠Donald ⁠Trump for disrespectful behaviour during national anthem.

US President Donald ⁠Trump criticised ⁠National Basketball Association (NBA) superstar LeBron James on Thursday for what he called disrespectful behaviour during the singing of the ⁠US national anthem at a recent NBA game.

“While listening to our National Anthem, LeBron James disrespects our Country,” Trump ⁠said in a Truth Social post accompanied by a video showing James moving his body during the anthem.

“LeBron James should apologize to all of those Great American Warriors ‌and Heroes who died for the American Flag, and all that our Country stands for!”

The clip Trump shared showed James standing in line with the members of the Philadelphia 76ers, swinging his arms in a warm-up-type stretch and performing basketball shooting movements.

A representative for the 76ers ⁠did not immediately respond to a ⁠request from Al Jazeera for comment.

Trump has repeatedly criticised athletes for their behaviour during pre-game renditions of the US national anthem, notably beginning with NFL quarterback Colin Kaepernick’s ⁠kneeling protest in support of racial justice.

Trump cancelled the planned White House visit of ⁠the Super Bowl champions Philadelphia Eagles ⁠in 2018 after the team disagreed with his call for players to stand during the anthem.

James became a leading voice in the Black Lives ‌Matter movement in 2020 and has frequently supported progressive issues as he ascended to the top of the NBA’s all-time ‌scoring ‌list.

news.originalContent:
The US has pushed back on the IRGC’s claims, dismissing them as an attempt to increase oil prices ahead of US elections.

Iran says that seven oil tankers have been struck and sustained damage in the Strait of Hormuz, the largest single-day toll for the waterway since the United States and Israel started their war against Iran on February 28.

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said in a statement on Thursday that four of the vessels were transferring oil when they were targeted and caught fire overnight. The other three were disabled after striking mines.

The claims could not be independently verified, and the report did not provide details about possible casualties or the tankers’ flags.

The IRGC also warned that it could strike US bases across the Middle East if Washington moves to help tankers transit other parts of the strait.

“The US military must know that if this trend continues, the conflict will extend to its bases in the region,” the IRGC said in a statement on its Sepah News website. “This is a serious warning.”

Iran claims control over Hormuz, a strategic shipping route through which one-fifth of the world’s oil supplies passed before war broke out. It regularly attacks ships that attempt to navigate the strait without its authorisation.

But the US military has been escorting vessels through the waterway in increasing numbers, with Iran responding by stepping up attacks.

US President Donald Trump said on Thursday that “Iran is doing everything they can to drive up the price of oil prior to the US Midterm Election”.

In a post on his Truth Social platform, he added: “They are making up fake hits, mines, and everything else because more oil is coming through the Hormuz Strait now than it did even prior to the beginning of the conflict.”

A US Central Command spokesperson, speaking anonymously to Al Jazeera, also called Iran’s mine claims incorrect.

The spokesperson said US forces have cleared the international shipping lanes of mines and that Iran is using missiles and drones.

The strait remains open, the spokesperson said, with 95 percent of vessels getting through.

The attacks, the spokesperson added, show Tehran’s “desperation” under the US blockade, which cuts Iran off from the resources it needs to rebuild the military capabilities the US has said it destroyed.

“The number of ships and tankers attacked every single day is increasing, and Iran is saying it is continuing to do this because they are not going to allow any change in that situation,” said Al Jazeera’s Mohamed Vall, reporting from Tehran.

“They have full control over the Strait of Hormuz right now, they say.”

Vall said there is also talk in Tehran about an imminent escalation in the war, with the Iranians expecting the US to attack even before US midterm elections in early November.

“The IRGC army chief has boasted that Iran is more ready than anytime before, and has produced enough weapons and equipment to wage a symmetrical war against the United States,” he said.

Reporting from the US White House, Al Jazeera’s Kimberly Halkett said: “Striking Iran does not appear to serve any Republican interests”, adding that pre-election polls tell the same story for Trump’s political party.

“What we’ve seen in surveys in recent months, and as of today, is that most Americans want relief from their tax money going to pay for any potential war with Iran that is ramped up,” Halkett said.

“There is real frustration over the rising cost for everyday Americans, given the rising fuel prices that have occurred as a result of this conflict  … As a result, the US president is having to make the case.

“The pressure is on the president, and it’s not just from the opposition party,” she said. “It is also from within the Republican Party as well.”

news.originalContent:
Illustration by Daily Caller Staff.

The Daily Caller’s website was discreetly censored as “misinformation,” and now everyone involved is playing the blame game.

A reader recently tried to access the Daily Caller’s website on the public WiFi at the Burlington International Airport in Vermont, which is municipally run. When the user tried to open an article, the reader was abruptly shown a prompt blocking the website as “Contentious & Misinformation.”

Jeff Bartley, the Director of Innovation and Marketing at the airport, assured the Caller they “absolutely did not block” the website.

“We are certainly not in the business attempting to dictate what is and should be blocked as ‘contentious or misinformation,’” Bartley told the Caller.

After confirming the prompt, which Bartley assumed was a glitch, he urgently made calls to resolve the issue. (RELATED: Republicans Cozying Up With Democrats To Save Liberals’ Favorite Censorship Agency)

Bartley suggested the Caller reach out to Purple WiFi, the airport’s WiFi carrier. Purple WiFi is a British company that provides WiFi for businesses and public venues, including the Burlington International Airport.

Purple WiFi told the Caller that the content was likely blocked because of content settings selected either by the airport or imposed by their third-party content-filter service, DNSFilter.

“While the defined categories are part of DNSFilter’s service, and so we use these to help customers define what ‘levels’ of filtering to apply, we do not set the categories that DNSFilter applies to a specified domain,” the carrier said.

In response to the Caller’s inquiry, Purple WiFi said they moved to have the website “whitelisted” on the airport’s domain.

DNSFilter is an AI-powered content filtering service that allows customers to restrict or specify the type of content users can access. DNSFilter has some categories that automatically filter things like “Adult Content” or “Terrorism and Hate,” while customers “set their own content policies” to block additional content.

The Caller was blocked as part of the “Contentious & Misinformation” category, which needs to be enabled by the customer.

“We don’t make editorial judgments about individual news outlets,” DNSFilter told the Caller.

Although they claimed not to make “editorial judgments,” DNSFilter admitted that they grouped the Daily Caller as part of the “misinformation” category.

“We group millions and millions of domains into categories for ease of management, so yes, those are samples of hundreds of categories that customers can choose from,” DNSFilter told the Caller. “What each customer chooses to filter as their policy is their choice.”

Although DNSFilter doesn’t enable the content filter themselves, they appear to encourage their customers to do so.

“The category is defined as sites that are contentious, often causing argument or controversy, characterized by strong opposing arguments, as well as sites that spread or aid in the spreading of misinformation,” the website reads. “This category can have a negative impact on productivity, as well as company culture.” (RELATED: Supreme Court Takes Up Landmark Government Censorship Case)

Evan Swarztrauber, principal at the telecom and technology industry consulting firm CorePoint Strategies, called DNSFilter “problematic” for filtering websites like the Daily Caller.

“DNSFilter touts over 57,000 organizations as customers,” Swarztrauber told the Caller. “It recommends a ‘misinformation’ filter to customers on an opt-in basis and reports that about 20 percent of its user base has it enabled. Its customer base includes large public WiFi networks, enterprise environments, and transportation hubs.”

“It is problematic from a free-speech standpoint that this company is apparently censoring conservative news outlets for thousands of customers while encouraging others to apply that same filter.”

DNSFilter has previously come under fire for alleged censorship. A recent report from Blaze News claimed that DNSFilter censored not only them and the Caller, but also other outlets like The Federalist, RedState, and One America News Network.

Nathan Leamer, founder of tech policy firm Fixed Gear Strategies and former FCC advisor, detailed how censorship typically targets conservative outlets.

“Across the Internet stack there are a number of choke points where gatekeepers can use their power to silence voices they do not like; most often we see this at the social media level,” Nathan Leamer, founder of Fixed Gear Strategies, told the Caller. “But down the Internet stack this is an issue that must be mitigated.” (RELATED: EXCLUSIVE: Legal Group Pushes For Transparency On USAID Involvement In Censorship During Biden Admin)

With all parties involved denying culpability and ultimately resolving the issue swiftly, it may be the case that the censorship was enabled at a lower level rather than a top-down corporate policy.

Preston Byrne, a free speech lawyer at Bryne & Storm, noted that UK businesses like Purple WiFi are “highly sensitive to political influence” given the lack of First Amendment or “jawboning” protections. Jawboning refers to informal attempts by government officials to strong-arm private companies into doing things like censoring speech, rather than using legal power or formal legislation.

Bryne also theorized that a potential culprit for the censorship could be a “rogue employee” rather than a top-down corporate policy.

“In my practice I have directly observed a handful of cases where private companies have formally blocked or deplatformed US-based companies because of those companies’ political orientation or their posture vis-à-vis UK content censorship,” Byrne told the Caller. “In this case, given the rapid remediation, we are more likely looking at a rogue employee than formal corporate policy action.”

This is hardly the first time outlets like the Caller have confronted censorship. In 2023, conservative outlets sued the State Department under former President Joe Biden for allegedly suppressing conservative speech online.

The joint lawsuit was filed by the Federalist, the Daily Wire, the New Civil Liberties Alliance (NCLA), and the state of Texas.

The State Department later settled the lawsuit in April 2026 and agreed to stop supporting the technology that censored conservatives.

news.originalContent:
(Photo by Amaury Cornu / Hans Lucas / AFP via Getty Images)

How many people, including celebrities, have threatened to leave the United States because of President Donald Trump since 2016? Many, as you might imagine. But how many actually got up and left? Far fewer. And of those who followed through, how many found joy, fulfillment and a better lifestyle? Even fewer, it seems.

Wired published a story Tuesday about Americans who moved to Europe in the wake of Trump’s second election win, only to regret the choice once their romanticized idea of what the Old World was like was shattered. (RELATED: Macron Hunts For Fuel Relief As Riots Rock France)

One influencer who focused on left-wing politics moved from New York to London in late 2024, after Trump won. However, she couldn’t land any British sponsorship deals because they didn’t think an American influencer would resonate with locals. She moved back earlier this year.

Another wannabe expat moved to Germany but has since returned to the U.S., where he feels “accepted and at home.” He also left because of Trump’s second term.

“Once I was in Germany and had some distance from the situation in the U.S., I felt perhaps I had overreacted,” he told the outlet.

One American woman lamented the poor quality of England’s National Health Service (NHS).

“I pay huge amounts of taxes and an immigration surcharge to access the NHS services—so no, the health care is not free here,” she said.

The best, though, is a New York art director who moved to Poland to escape right-wing populism. Of course, there he found that right-wing politics and conservatism are even more popular than in the United States.

“What is happening in the US is also happening everywhere now, to the point I’m even a little hesitant in what I say to you, or anywhere online,” he told Wired, saying that he feels trapped in Europe, along with his Polish wife and young child.

Although not mentioned in Wired’s story, an American transgender from San Francisco recently claimed asylum in the Netherlands. He ended up stuck in a fenced-off immigration internment camp. Allegedly, Dutch customs officers laughed off the asylum request.

“They laughed because: what’s this big dumb American doing here asking about asylum? And then they realized I was serious,” 47-year-old Jane-Michelle Arc said.

Europe, particularly France, is certainly not an ideal place to be trapped in as rioting and social unrest ripple across the continent. After decades of unchecked immigration, Paris is no longer the city that famous American expats, like Ernest Hemingway and F. Scott Fitzgerald, called home. The same goes for London, Berlin, and Brussels.

Vacationing in a wealthy European tourist destination is not a bad way to spend two weeks. But living there year-round? You will get the real experience. Unfortunately for these naive and overreactive Americans, they messed around and eventually found out.

Although not mentioned in Wired’s story, an American transgender from San Francisco recently claimed asylum in the Netherlands. He ended up stuck in a fenced-off immigration internment camp. Allegedly, Dutch customs officers laughed off the asylum request.

“They laughed because: what’s this big dumb American doing here asking about asylum? And then they realized I was serious,” 47-year-old Jane-Michelle Arc said.

Europe, particularly France, is certainly not an ideal place to be trapped in as rioting and social unrest ripple across the continent. After decades of unchecked immigration, Paris is no longer the city that famous American expats, like Ernest Hemingway and F. Scott Fitzgerald, called home. The same goes for London, Berlin, and Brussels.

Vacationing in a wealthy European tourist destination is not a bad way to spend two weeks. But living there year-round? You will get the real experience. Unfortunately for these naive and overreactive Americans, they messed around and eventually found out.

Moving to a new city may be an easy cash grab.

Topeka, Kansas has announced a new relocation incentive program where eligible folks who pack up and head to the Midwest can score up to $15,000 in cold, hard cash. You’ll have to do some work, though, as the program — called Choose Topeka — is tied to Shawnee County employers.

As with all free funds, the capital of Kansas has some requirements before it doles out the cash. The city is urging folks to take a few steps before even applying.

For example, anyone who fills out the form must secure a job with a Shawnee County employer to even be considered eligible. But be sure to check with your new job before making any moves, as not every employer offers relocation incentives — participation is voluntary and position-specific.

The historic city — which has a population of 178,941 — said that the relocation program is typically reserved for “hard-to-fill roles” which likely require specialized skills, education or experience. However, the program is open to all employers, with over 50 companies participating today.

In order to be eligible for the moolah, you must meet four requirements, according to the website:

The green is limited to one person per household — so an entire family will not be able to claim more than $15,000.

The county also has reserved cash for what it calls “boomerang” applicants. These are individuals who previously lived in Shawnee County, moved away, but now interested in returning to live and work in the community.

Kansas is one of the most historic states in the US as Topeka delivered the landmark Brown v. Board of Education. The Supreme Court’s 1954 milestone decision ruled separating children in public schools on the basis of race was unconstitutional.

In addition to its rich history, the city — located about 60 miles due west of Kansas City — has an interesting art scene where Trip Advisor deemed Truckhenge — a “Stonehenge-like” travel destination — a must-see.

Created by Ron Lessman beginning in 2000, the outdoor grassroots art installation has six antique trucks planted firmly in the ground, nose-first in a circular arrangement. The installation is on the Lessman family farm between Tecumseh and Topeka, Kansas.

The town also has award-winning beer as the Blind Tiger Brewery and Restaurant took home the 2012 World Beer Cup Gold Award for Maibock beer. The famed spot has also won 15 gold, silver or bronze medals at the Great American Beer Festival and the World Beer Cup — dubbed the Olympics of Beer.

So, if you’re having second thoughts about your city or just waiting on a reason to scram, Topeka’s relocation program might be your ticket out.

news.originalContent:
See more of our coverage in your search results.

Caleb Williams is back and the market is awfully eager to crown the Bears after topping the fickle Falcons by one possession.

In the three games the dynamic gunslinger was absent due to a hamstring injury, the Bears found themselves primarily relying on their defense. That’s not to discredit Case Keenum’s resurrection on “Monday Night Football” against the Eagles in Week 3, but red-zone struggles were a theme across that span: Chicago scored just four times across 15 trips inside the opponent’s 20-yard line.

Mind you, this is a defense that allows an NFL-worst 6 yards per play.

Williams certainly gave the market good reason to trust him in his rust-free return against Atlanta. He orchestrated touchdown drives in the Bears’ first two drives and finished the day with 305 yards, an 83 percent completion rate, and zero turnovers.

A fellow 4-2 Patriots team that is really in its stride right now represents a different challenge for Williams and the Bears on Thursday.

I’ll be the first to admit I hit the eject button on New England after the Jaguars decimated them by 29 points. Their cakewalk of a schedule that mapped them to the Super Bowl last year felt like it was beginning to get exposed.

But since then, Drake Maye’s turnover issues have completely vanished. After throwing six interceptions through three weeks, the MVP runner-up has tossed an NFL-best 10 touchdowns against just one interception over his last three games. Maye is also leading the league in passer rating (119.3) and EPA per dropback (0.38) during that stretch.

These numbers aren’t inflated by one favorable matchup, either. Maye helped engineer these victories with a 47-point explosion over a respectable Raiders team and is the only challenger to best Josh Allen thus far.

It’s worth mentioning that New England’s offensive line is battered on the short week. It lost Morgan Moses and Alijah Vera-Tucker to injuries against the Jets, while Mike Onwenu and Greg Van Roten are already on injured reserve.

The Bears pressure within the top five defenses, so Maye will need to get the football out of his hands when he can. Even so, the Patriots allowed zero sacks and just four quarterback hits against the Jets despite losing three offensive linemen in the game.

Establishing the run game will be key. New England churned out 148 rushing yards against the Jets, and it’s helpful that Chicago ranks among the bottom five in yards allowed before contact on running plays.

I also expect a bounce-back effort from A.J. Brown. The star wideout managed only three catches on 10 targets in his first full game with the Patriots. His role won’t be going anywhere.

Perhaps the biggest differentiator between these two is New England’s defense, which ranks among the league’s top 10 in both points and yards allowed.

The Patriots do rely heavily on man coverage — a scheme that Williams ranks within the top three in both completion percentage and passer rating against. Whether defensive coordinator Zak Kuhr mixes in more zone coverage remains to be seen, though I expect cornerback Christian Gonzalez, who ranks 11th overall in passer rating allowed per Pro Football Focus, to limit one side of the field either way.

This is one of the bigger toss-up Thursday night games of the season, so side with the more capable defense and a Patriots team that’s 5-1-1 against the spread as road underdogs under Mike Vrabel.

THE PLAY: Patriots +2.5 (+125, 45 percent, Polymarket)

news.originalContent:
See more of our coverage in your search results.

Los Angeles voters are facing a grim choice in the race for mayor, with some so disillusioned by Karen Bass’ leadership that they are backing her for another four years simply because they believe her challenger would be even worse.

The California Post spoke to voters across Los Angeles on Tuesday, October 20, with many expressing frustration over the city’s spiraling homelessness crisis, soaring cost of living, public safety problems and the response to the devastating Palisades Fire.

But despite their frustration with Bass, some said they would reluctantly vote for the incumbent rather than risk handing City Hall to Councilwoman Nithya Raman, who has been endorsed by the Democratic Socialists of America.

Among them is Hollywood writer Heidi Van Tassell, who made headlines in 2019 after a homeless man attacked her on Hollywood Boulevard and dumped a bucket of hot feces over her head.

Van Tassell, who said she knew people who lost their homes in the wildfires, was deeply disappointed in Bass but feared Raman would be worse.

“I’ve had friends who’ve lost their homes in the fire and I’m just disappointed in her, but now I’m voting for her because Spencer Pratt is not in it anymore,” she said.

“I’d rather have four more years of her than eight years of Nithya Raman.”

Van Tassell said she had spoken to Raman about homelessness but came away with little confidence in her plans to tackle the crisis.

“(Raman) rolled her eyes and said, ‘we’re done here,'” Van Tassell recalled.

Despite describing LA as “a great city,” Van Tassell feared it was becoming increasingly dystopian, comparing it to the apocalyptic Hollywood movie “Escape from L.A.”

Business owner AJ Johnson also said he would vote for Bass, describing her as the better of two mediocre choices.

Johnson said something as simple as cleaning up the city’s trash-strewn streets could go a long way toward restoring public confidence in City Hall.

Other voters were so unimpressed by the choice that they wished they could write in another candidate altogether.

Saleswoman Linda Mintz said she would rather vote for tech entrepreneur Adam Miller or real estate developer Rick Caruso, who lost to Bass in the 2022 mayoral election.

Mintz praised Caruso, the developer behind The Grove shopping center, for his hands-on approach to running the popular LA destination.

“I actually wish Caruso was running again because I really like that man and I go to the Grove all the time,” she said.

“I mean if the fountain isn’t on, he goes ‘how come the fountain’s not on? Music? How come the music’s not on? One call and everything happens.”

For these frustrated Angelenos, the question is not necessarily who can make Los Angeles better, but which candidate they trust least to make it worse.

Watch the video to hear what voters had to say about the mayoral race and what needs to change in Los Angeles.

It’s been quite a week for Kylie Jenner.

After walking in her first Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show on Sunday night — wearing the iconic $50,000,000 Fantasy Bra, no less — Kylie is now the new face of Stella McCartney.

The 29-year-old makeup mogul stars alongside a trained horse on the beach at sunset in a short film that was directed by legendary filmmaker Gia Coppola.

“From archival collections to the winter 2026 runway, the horse has remained a defining symbol of the house,” The brand writes their website.

Titled “Wild Horses,” the brand states “the film is an ode to the power, sensitivity and freedom of the horse” in a press release.

In the shots, Jenner slips into a wispy black lace-paneled camisole ($1,575), chainmail halter top ($1,990), purple peplum mini dress ($1,990) and more.

The press release continues, “Horses are part of Stella McCartney’s foundation: a lifelong connection rooted in Stella’s childhood, her family and a belief that fashion must recognize humanity as part of nature, rather than separate from it.”

And they address their choice of model, stating, “The casting for this Icon Series carries its own Stella juxtaposition: Kylie – an icon of contemporary femininity and unapologetic glamour – is taken out of the expected and immersed in the raw beauty of our natural world, celebrating the unique space our brand holds.”

This is not the first time a Jenner has modeled with horses for their friend Stella.

In fact, for the brand’s winter 2023 campaign, older sister Kendall Jenner posed for a similar shoot, surrounded by white Camargue horses. It was, aptly, shot in the Camargue Salt Flats in France.

At the time, Kendall shared, “Humans and horses have been reliable partners throughout history, and that mutual trust over time is probably why our connection is so powerful.”

Though Kylie has been dipping her toe into the modeling world — previously walking the runway for Coperni and posing in ad campaigns for Skims, Alo and more — she’s adding another high-fashion notch to her belt.

news.originalContent:
La Liga ⁠chief ⁠Javier Tebas compared Real Madrid’s communication to Nazi propaganda and now faces a tribunal in Spain.

La Liga President Javier Tebas could face disciplinary action for comparing Real Madrid’s communication methods with those of Nazi propaganda minister Joseph Goebbels, after Spain’s National Sports Council (CSD) asked the country’s sports tribunal on Thursday to assess whether the football executive had committed an offence.

The CSD said in a statement that it had referred the matter to the country’s Administrative Court for Sport (TAD) after Tebas made the comparison in a post on social media platform X on October 16.

The TAD must determine whether Tebas’s comments could constitute a serious offence under Spain’s 1990 Sports Law, which includes “notorious and public acts that harm sporting dignity or decorum”.

The CSD said, “It is essential to preserve the values that make sport a space of respect, coexistence, and fair play.”

Spanish giants Real Madrid called for Tebas, 64, to resign after he criticised their efforts to discredit refereeing in Spain.

Tebas had said Real Madrid’s in-house TV channel often suggested that referees attempt to prevent the club from winning.

The outspoken Spanish league chief said these tactics “recall propaganda mechanisms exploited by Goebbels”.

Tebas later attempted to clarify that he was drawing comparisons with “those propaganda techniques” and not with the ideology of the Nazis.

The La Liga chief reiterated on Thursday with another X post that his comment had “distinguished between propaganda techniques and ideology”.

Tebas also questioned why Madrid, in “accusing the refereeing system of corruption”, did “not affect sporting dignity and decorum”.

“Does it not harm clubs, referees, and millions of fans?” wrote Tebas. “Or do those values only deserve a public defence when someone responds to such attacks?”

Real Madrid criticise referees most weeks on their television channel, and last year accused officiating in Spain of being “rigged” and “totally discredited”.

La Liga ‌did ‌not immediately respond to a request for comment.

news.originalContent:
Young Serbians have built a system that poses a threat to President Aleksandar Vucic’s grip on power.

It all began on the streets.

A student-led movement has emerged as the most serious challenger to the long rule of the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) and its leader, Aleksandar Vucic, ahead of Sunday’s election.

Over the past two years, many citizens, teachers, professors and other experts have joined the students, a protest group that has evolved into a political movement: “Student List–Students Win” (Studentska lista–Studenti pobeđuju).

The catalyst came after the collapse of a concrete canopy at the renovated Novi Sad railway station on November 1, 2024. Sixteen people were killed in the tragedy, which triggered public outrage over alleged corruption and raised questions about construction safety, the quality of renovation work, and government oversight. Students who led protests have sought a fundamental overhaul of a system they deem rotten.

Kosta Golubovic, a law student at the University of Novi Sad, has been involved since day one.

“Change is clearly necessary. The state must belong to its people, not to the mafia and criminals,” he told Al Jazeera.

“The way they treat the judiciary, the catastrophic conditions at the local level, mayors resorting to violence, dying villages – along with dubious privatisations, money laundering, the erosion of every single institution, police being replaced by thugs, and an education system vanishing before our eyes… these are some of the reasons why change is needed,” said Golubovic.

Demonstrations transformed into the biggest protest movement in Serbia in years, joined by tens of thousands.

The students have not called for the overthrow of Vucic. But their persistence created one of the biggest threats to the president’s long grip on power.

Vucic became prime minister in 2014. In 2017, he was elected president, a traditionally ceremonial role that he has bolstered by maintaining influence over his SNS party.

Opposition parties and rights watchdogs accuse Vucic and his SNS party of bribing voters, stifling media freedom, violence against opponents, and ties with organised crime.

Vucic and his allies deny these allegations. But Serbia’s rating on Transparency International’s global corruption index has worsened gradually in recent years.

“Vucic is clearly afraid of us – it’s obvious. He knows that, for the first time in 16 years, the SNS is no longer the most popular political option in the country,” Golubovic said.

The students’ efficiency is down in part to its structure.

The old student parliament at the University of Belgrade has been replaced with plenums – daily assemblies where each group votes on its course of action. Working groups focus on strategy, donations, and security. Universities in different cities coordinate so demands remain broadly aligned.

This is why the students say they do things differently. One rule is to be leaderless, making it harder for authorities to disrupt the protests. Also, demonstrations must be peaceful, and any debris has to be cleaned up. Third, all decisions must be made democratically during hour-long plenary sessions in their university faculties.

“Even though the authorities mobilised criminal groups against the students and citizens participating in the protests, the students have remained focused on their goal: to oust a government they view as authoritarian and deeply corrupt,” said Natasa Kandic, a Serbian peace activist, sociologist, and founder of the Humanitarian Law Center (HLC) in Belgrade.

“For the first time in Serbia, they have managed to lead protests entirely without violence,” she said. “The video clips we see daily represent a new culture – one defined by irony, laughter, and the deliberate disregard for primitivism and political depravity.”

State-affiliated media have maligned the students. Some Serbian authorities claimed that the group has no programme, and Vucic labelled them as “terrorists”. But their leaders, experts from different fields, claim that they have a plan.

The platform is officially titled the “Student Plan” and is divided into three sections. There are 11 points.

Ilija Srdanovic, a cardiologist and the lead candidate and ballot holder for the Student List, explained that the platform deliberately avoids setting fixed, precise deadlines for the proposed changes. He argued that such timelines can only be determined once contributors have gained insight into the “full current state of affairs”.

“[We plan] many things – too many to list – but the goal is to change the system,” said Srdanovic in a brief call to Al Jazeera.

During debates, the establishment of a special prosecutorial police unit, a law on the origin of assets, transitional justice and the renovation of rural medical clinics are some frequent themes.

Could this be implemented in the case of a victory? Kandic is sceptical.

“The student movement doesn’t possess a transformative potential – the capacity to drive social change, break with the past, and alter a political climate where convicted war criminals are celebrated, Kosovo is treated as part of Serbia, and politicians from neighboring countries are branded as enemies,” he said.

Hope Hooton and Kellie Elliott feared their children were not safe with their fathers. Hope sought protection after her husband threatened suicide and later experienced a psychiatric crisis. Kellie documented years of domestic violence and abuse. Yet both fathers had unsupervised time with their children, whom they later killed.

Through the stories of these two mothers, Fault Lines investigates how evidence of danger can be missed, dismissed or fail to reach family courts at all. The film examines the push for equal custody, the failure to treat violence against a parent as a risk to children and the changes advocates say could prevent other families from suffering the same losses.

news.originalContent:
Rising costs leave US workers juggling multiple jobs as financial security becomes increasingly elusive.

Stacy Eichel, an empty nester in Florida, spent years balancing two jobs. One was in healthcare; the other was her own venture: a small business making custom-branded merchandise for corporate clients, such as coffee mugs and T-shirts that companies hand out at conferences and holiday parties.

For Eichel, the business was more than a paycheque. It was a side hustle for a woman who couldn’t sit still, who was always hungry for the next opportunity. It was the kind of business that thrived when companies had a little extra to spend on small branded trinkets to make an otherwise mundane corporate conference something memorable.

In September 2025, Eichel lost her job in marketing for a healthcare company after a merger. Suddenly, the business she had run on the side had to shoulder more of the burden of supporting her. Yet just as she needed it to provide more, the market for her products was shrinking.

Faced with uncertainty over trade policy and tariffs, alongside the growing use of artificial intelligence across the economy, companies have been tightening their spending. Custom-branded merchandise was becoming one more expense they could do without.

“The economy is such that fewer people are buying custom-branded swag because it’s more of a luxury item. When they have extra money in the budget, that’s what they’ll use it for, but now their budgets are very tight,” Eichel, who has cut back on her expenses, told Al Jazeera.

Eichel’s experience reflects a broader strain in the US labour market, where a paycheque does not necessarily translate into financial security. The headline unemployment rate captures people actively looking for work, but it does not tell the whole story of people who are working fewer hours than they want or juggling jobs that do not provide enough income.

The Department of Labor documents this through what is called the U-6 rate, a broader measure of unemployment and underemployment. It stands at an elevated 7.6 percent. While that’s down from 8.1 percent a year ago, having a job does not necessarily mean Americans are getting ahead financially.

The U-6 measure includes people who are working part-time because they cannot find full-time jobs, as well as those who want to work but have stopped looking for a job recently.

Even people who are employed full-time are finding that their earnings do not stretch as far as they once did. An estimated 4.5 million Americans were working part-time because they could not find full-time work. Meanwhile, nine million Americans held multiple jobs, accounting for 5.5 percent of all employed workers, according to the most recent jobs report.

“Underemployment is one of the most misunderstood economic problems in America because it doesn’t always look like unemployment. It looks like a college graduate working retail despite having a degree, a former executive accepting a position paying half their previous salary, or a parent working two jobs because neither provides enough hours, benefits or income to support their family,” Tara Furiani, a workforce strategist based in Richmond, Virginia, told Al Jazeera.

Average hourly wages rose 3 percent over the past year, while consumer prices increased 3.7 percent, according to the latest Consumer Price Index (CPI) report released by the US Labor Department.

That means prices have risen faster than wages, leaving many workers with less purchasing power. Overall, prices rose 0.6 percent from the previous month, while average hourly wages increased by just 0.1 percent, adding to the financial pressure on households like Eichel’s.

Eichel has cut back on expenses and scaled down some of her usual spending, including dining out and takeout, and dropped her cable service.

“I never used to think before ordering in, and now we cook everything,” Eichel said.

With the midterm elections approaching, the cost of living is becoming a greater concern for voters. A Reuters/Ipsos poll found that the cost of living was the most important issue for voters, leading the next-closest issue by a double-digit margin, at 47 percent compared with 22 percent for “democratic norms and values”.

A separate Washington Post–ABC News–Ipsos poll found that voters trust Democrats over Republicans to handle the economy, 40 percent to 33 percent, marking the first time in 12 years that Democrats have held an advantage on the issue.

This comes as 44 percent of Americans said they had struggled to pay for at least one basic necessity over the past year, including transportation, rent or mortgage payments, medical care and food, according to a Pew Research Center poll released earlier this month.

Twenty percent of respondents said they had received food from a food bank or pantry over the past year.

news.originalContent:
On trade, investment and innovation, leaders will work towards conclusion of a Canada-Turkiye Free Trade Agreement.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan have announced the launch of a Canada-Turkiye Strategic Partnership, backed by a three-year action plan.

“In an increasingly complex global security environment, rising geopolitical uncertainties, and evolving humanitarian challenges, a strong and resilient Canada-Turkiye partnership is essential, providing a foundation to mitigate shared threats and capitalise on new opportunities,” said a statement by the two leaders on Thursday.

This comes as Carney is on a two-day visit to Turkiye, seeking to forge a new partnership as Canada looks to reduce its dependence on the United States.

The partnership’s three-year action plan rests on four pillars: trade and investment; defence and security; energy; and ties between people, the statement said.

On trade, investment and innovation, the two leaders agreed to “work toward successful conclusion of a Canada-Turkiye Free Trade Agreement”, it said. They will also expand bilateral trade and investments in priority sectors, including energy supply, defence production, aerospace, and artificial intelligence (AI).

On defence and security, the leaders “underlined their intent to deepen bilateral and multilateral cooperation”. They also agreed to “strengthen cooperation in support of peace and security in the Euro-Atlantic region and beyond including Ukraine, South Caucasus, and the Middle East, in particular Gaza”.

Meanwhile, energy ministers from both countries will work on areas such as liquefied natural gas, nuclear energy and critical minerals.

Speaking to reporters in Ankara alongside Carney on Thursday, Erdogan said the two countries “hope to increase our trade volume, which currently stands at around $3bn, to $5bn initially and then to $10bn through the steps we will take”.

He said the two sides had agreed to begin free trade agreement negotiations before the end of the year to boost trade and investment, adding that elevating Turkiye-Canada relations to the level of a strategic partnership would not be merely a symbolic step on paper.

“We have today overcome the disconnect that had persisted between Turkiye and Canada for many years. Now, we are launching a new era between Turkiye and Canada,” he said.

Canadian and Turkish leaders will convene next month in Ankara for the first round of trade talks, the joint statement said.
Carney is on the first bilateral visit by a Canadian prime minister to Turkiye, although he travelled to Ankara in July to attend the NATO summit.

He was scheduled to meet Erdogan and other officials before travelling to Istanbul for talks with Turkish business groups as the two countries seek to deepen trade ties.

The Canadian prime minister has sought to diversify partnerships and reduce reliance on the US amid an escalating trade war with US President Donald Trump, marked by US tariffs on Canadian goods, followed by retaliatory measures from Canada, as well as Trump’s statements questioning Canadian sovereignty.

news.originalContent:
Israel can inflict devastating damage on Iran, but analysts question its ability to overthrow Tehran’s government.

Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said that overthrowing Iran’s government remains Israel’s “primary objective”, as he faces declining support in the polls before national elections next week.

His remarks came after conversations with United States President Donald Trump on Sunday and a visit to Israel by Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth. But Netanyahu offered no indication that Washington had agreed to join another offensive against Iran, let alone a campaign to bring down Iran’s leadership.

While Israel has the firepower to inflict serious damage on Iran, analysts told Al Jazeera, it lacks a clear strategy for translating military gains into the overthrow of Iran’s government. Air strikes alone are unlikely to achieve that objective, while a ground invasion would demand a far greater military commitment, they said.

A renewed offensive would also mean confronting a state that has already survived two rounds of attacks and retains the means to retaliate – both against Israel and its Gulf neighbours who are hosting US military assets. US backing, meanwhile, remains uncertain, with experts questioning Washington’s appetite for renewed fighting as it is yet to find a credible prospect of forcing Iran’s government to surrender to its demands.

Israel’s ability to attack Iran is not in doubt, experts say. Urban Coningham, a research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), told Al Jazeera that its offensive weapons stockpiles, and “aerial refuelling” capabilities give it a substantial advantage. “Israel could again establish air superiority and strike Iranian targets,” he said.

But while Israel can inflict serious damage, analysts are sceptical that it can accomplish regime change.

Netanyahu has portrayed Iran’s leaders as a major threat since his first term as prime minister in 1996. Addressing the US Congress that July, he said, “The most dangerous of these regimes is Iran, that has wed a cruel despotism to a fanatic militancy.”

Nearly 30 years later, US participation in the June 2025 war, and again in the campaign launched on February 28 this year, delivered the military intervention Netanyahu had long sought. The overthrow of Iran’s government, however, did not follow. Netanyahu himself acknowledged the limits of airpower in March, saying, “You can’t do it only from the air.”

“There has to be a ground component, as well,” he added, without explaining what that would involve.

Caglar Kurc, an assistant professor at Abdullah Gul University in Kayseri, Turkiye, said bombing could weaken Iran’s military but not necessarily eliminate its ability to fight back. “Airpower can degrade military capabilities but cannot fully destroy offensive capabilities,” he told Al Jazeera. “Well-hidden systems would survive.”

Overthrowing the government, Kurc said, would require a willingness to deploy troops and remain on the ground for years. Israel can also no longer assume that covert methods used in earlier attacks would prove equally effective again.

Coningham described intelligence assets as “use and burn” because deploying these methods risks exposing networks that Iranian security services will investigate and disrupt.

Israel still has “human intelligence assets on the ground”, he said, while “cyberattacks” could also form part of another campaign. But using those capabilities risks revealing and sacrificing them, making the prospect of a tangible military gain an important consideration.

Covert operations and cyberattacks, in his assessment, do not offer a clear route to overthrowing Iran’s government. Coningham was similarly sceptical that Kurdish or Baloch armed groups could provide the ground force needed to challenge the state. In March, the Trump administration was said to be actively discussing providing arms to opposition Kurdish groups, according to CNN, which cited Kurdish and US officials. But this never progressed.

“Kurdish groups lacked the military capabilities to take on the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC),” he said.

Iran also does not need to match Israel aircraft-for-aircraft to make another offensive very costly, experts say.

Sidharth Kaushal, a senior research fellow at RUSI, told Al Jazeera that the “Iranians likely retain sizeable stocks of missiles,” even if damage to their targeting systems may constrain their effectiveness.

“The actual antiship missile stockpiles likely remain large, both because they are comparatively easy to make, and Iran has in-housed much of the production of older Chinese ASCMs, and Iran’s southern mountains provide natural shelters against air attack,” Kaushal said.

Coningham said that, for Israel, sustaining its defences would be more difficult, with previous exchanges having drawn down interceptor stocks.

Repeated attacks also impose a financial burden, as Israel will be intercepting relatively inexpensive Iranian drones with far more costly defensive weapons. Over a prolonged exchange, that imbalance could place further pressure on Israel’s interceptor supplies, while Iran retains the capacity to mass-produce more cheap weapons for a lot longer.

Analysts consider this unlikely, pointing to diverging political interests between Tel Aviv and Washington, with Trump facing pressure to avoid renewed escalation before the US midterm elections.

The Financial Times reported this week that an Israeli proposal for renewed strikes had failed to secure Trump’s approval, although it suggested disagreement about immediate action rather than Washington ruling out future attacks altogether.

Without Trump’s participation, Coningham said, Israel would lack US capabilities for striking deeply buried facilities. These include the 30,000-pound GBU-57 bunker-busting bombs that US B-2 bombers dropped on Iran’s Fordow and Natanz nuclear facilities in June 2025. Designed to penetrate deeply buried targets, the weapons gave Washington an offensive capability Israel could not match on its own.

Coningham also suggested that, if Israel were to attack without US support, Iran might concentrate its retaliation on Israeli territory while avoiding US targets and disruption to the Strait of Hormuz.

Such an approach would seek to punish Israel without drawing Washington directly into the fighting, potentially further isolating a country already widely ostracised by the international community amid its genocide in Gaza.

But analysts say the central obstacle that could ultimately prevent Israel from attacking Iran is the gap between its ability to destroy military targets and its capacity to force political change within Iran.

“You cannot change a regime unless you are prepared to deploy troops and stay in the country for some years. Israel cannot control Iran. The United States would not engage in another regime change, which could take decades,” Kurc added.

news.originalContent:
Military has raised the threat level of ​Russian sabotage against German troops and facilities.

A Ukrainian national has been arrested in Germany on suspicion of spying for Russia, German authorities have said.

Germany’s federal prosecutors confirmed in a statement on Thursday that the man, identified as Vadym Y, was arrested in the state of Brandenburg 85km (53 miles) west of Berlin.

Prosecutors said the suspect had been in touch with the Russian secret service via an intermediary since at least July 2025.

The suspect had gathered military intelligence on the production of armoured vehicles, ammunition and explosives, as well as military personnel and defence installations at locations designed to secure NATO’s eastern flank, prosecutors added.

news.originalContent:
(Getty Images/Brendan Smialowski)

Three soldiers were awarded with Purple Hearts and given special recognition for their efforts providing aid to other wounded U.S. service members during an Iranian attack on a U.S. airbase.

The U.S. awarded Staff Sgt. Kalob Mitchell, Sgt. Xavier Jones and Spc. Nicholas Cabo of the 6th Battalion, 56th Air Defense Artillery Regiment with Purple Hearts for their efforts to help rescue others during a March 27 attack at the Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia. At the ceremony, the trio’s Unit Commander, Capt. Tyler Ritter, read thank you notes from those they saved, Stars and Stripes reported Tuesday.

Less than a month after the Iran War began, the “Alarm Red” siren turned on at the Prince Sultan Airbase, warning that an Iranian attack from across the Persian Gulf may be imminent, the outlet reported. Suddenly, a 550 lb. Iranian ballistic missile landed near their bunker, sending out shock and sonic waves.

“Everything went black,” Mitchell told Stars and Stripes. “We’d been hit.” (RELATED: Soldiers Wounded In Iran War Reportedly Failed By Medical System)

Video footage purported to show an Iranian ballistic missile strike on Prince Sultan Air Base in Al-Kharj, Saudi Arabia, with the missile impacting very close to several U.S. servicemembers, thankfully said to have resulted in only minor injuries to personnel at Prince Sultan. https://t.co/Nlju8TCZ22

After another soldier awakened them, the three quickly sprung into action.

“[W]e heard screams from the opposite side of the bunker. Two soldiers, I’m not too sure who they were, had significant injuries; (we) ran over there, applied tourniquets, T Triple C (Tactical Combat Casualty Care), everything,” Mitchell recounted to Stars and Stripes.

Mitchell, Cabo, and Jones gave aid to a gravely injured soldier, treated one with a neck injury and helped calm another that became disoriented from the blast, the outlet reported.

“I think it was just the adrenaline because, after we woke up, I checked myself,” Cabo told Stars and Stripes, “I just saw that my leg was a little bit bleeding, so I didn’t really mind it. It wasn’t anything like crazy bleeding, so we just heard screams and went to go help those guys.”

It is unclear how many were wounded during the attack. As of Wednesday, the Defense Casualty Analysis System has recorded 21 killed and 865 wounded since the Iran war began on Feb. 28.

Multiple American military installations have been hit during the Iranian conflict. These strikes have amounted to billions of dollars of damage to military installations, embassies, and other diplomatic facilities. Hundreds of buildings within the American defense infrastructure have been damaged as a result.

news.originalContent:

An e-bike rider is clinging to life after he was struck by a hit-and-run driver on a busy Brooklyn street Tuesday night, cops said.

The 33-year-old biker was riding south in the right lane on Nostrand Avenue near Atlantic Avenue in Crown Heights – a buzzing commercial intersection – around 7:30 p.m. when he was struck by the driver of a white 2026 Hyundai Elantra, police said.

The Elantra driver had been in the center lane before beginning to merge into the right lane, where the crash happened, authorities said.

The cyclist was thrown from the bike onto the pavement and suffered head trauma, according to cops.

He was rushed to the Kings County Hospital Center, where he remained in critical condition Wednesday, police said.

The Hyundai driver fled the scene, heading south on Nostrand Avenue, and remained on the lam, police said.

The crash comes weeks after a man riding an e-bike was fatally struck by a pick-up truck driver in the Bronx, cops and sources said.

The 50-year-old biker was heading west on East 145th Street when the truck driver, traveling south on Brook Avenue in Mott Haven, hit him around 8:25 a.m. Oct. 7, according to authorities and law enforcement sources.

The pick-up truck driver, a 55-year-old man, stayed at the scene and did not face any charges, police said.

And last month, a delivery woman was killed when a dump truck plowed into her e-bike and then drove off in the heart of Herald Square, according to cops and an advocacy group.

The truck driver collided with the 50-year-old cyclist the morning of Sept. 28, as both headed west on West 34th Street, approaching Seventh Avenue, police said.

The woman — who was riding a JOCO rental e-bike and making a delivery — was pronounced dead at the scene.

news.originalContent:
